supportingExcerpt: The mitochondrial route uses BCL-2-family control of BAX and BAK and cytochrome c release. In cell experiments, combined BAX and BAK loss blocked mitochondrial responses to several apoptotic stimuli; this does not establish resistance to all forms of death. Death-receptor signals provide another route. Apoptosis is not inherently immune-silent: anthracycline-treated tumour cells showed calreticulin-dependent immunogenicity in mouse experiments. A death marker, a mitochondrial response and sustained killing answer different questions. Protein abundance alone cannot establish dependence or choose a treatment.

The BCL-2 family contains survival proteins, including BCL-2, BCL-XL and MCL-1; BH3-only stress mediators, including BIM, BID and PUMA; and pore-forming effectors BAX and BAK. In experimental cells, loss of both BAX and BAK blocked several mitochondrial apoptotic responses, rather than every possible form of death.

Cytochrome c moves from the mitochondrial intermembrane compartment, including crista stores, across the outer membrane to the cytosol. It does not begin in the matrix. The inner membrane separates these compartments; the spatial sketch is simplified, with no implied pore stoichiometry.

Intrinsic apoptosis involves mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation, cytochrome c release into the cytosol, apoptosome assembly and caspase-9 activation upstream of executioner caspases such as caspase-3 and caspase-7. Death-receptor signalling can activate caspase-8; BID cleavage links this route to mitochondria. Initiator and executioner roles differ.

A stain for BCL-XL measures abundance rather than survival dependence. BCL2 and BCL2L1 are different genes, and inhibitor selectivity matters. Souers and colleagues re-engineered dual BCL-2/BCL-XL inhibition into BCL-2-selective ABT-199, sparing human platelets; early tumour lysis in three refractory chronic lymphocytic leukaemia patients does not establish benefit in every tumour. A mitochondrial response, caspase marker, sustained killing and immune protection remain separate outcomes. Keep cell identity, timing, handling controls and later survival or regrowth with cleaved-caspase assays, membrane readouts and microscopy. Mitochondrial BH3 challenges test readiness under a defined protocol, rather than completed killing or clinical benefit.

Compare mechanism, morphology, immune consequence and living arrest separately. Apoptosis uses regulated dismantling; necrotic morphology describes boundary failure; ferroptosis requires iron-dependent lipid damage causing death; immunogenicity requires a compatible adaptive response; senescence is a living arrest. These categories are not mutually exclusive outcomes or a universal appearance-based classifier.

The 2020 consensus defines immunogenic cell death through the adaptive immune response, not merely the appearance of dead cells. Antigens, appropriately timed danger signals, antigen-presenting cells and a responsive host all matter. Apoptotic or other death machinery does not by itself classify the immune outcome.

Calreticulin exposure, ATP or HMGB1 release and interferon-related signals are useful mechanistic readouts, but none alone proves protective immunity. Functional cross-priming and appropriate in-vivo immune tests address later steps. The consensus distinguishes mouse vaccination models from established disease; neither a surrogate marker nor a positive mouse assay establishes clinical benefit in a person.

In a local-treatment study, follow injury and signals through presentation, priming, recognition and measured tumour outcomes. Circulating cytokines or proliferating T cells alone do not establish tumour-specific killing, distant control or an optimal radiation dose.

Immunogenic cell death is regulated death capable of initiating antigen-specific adaptive immunity in a compatible responding host. Antigenicity and appropriately timed adjuvant signals are both necessary considerations. It is an immune consequence, not an exclusive machine opposed to apoptosis or necrotic appearance.

In the consensus vaccination assay, remove residual inducing chemical and add no separate adjuvant before vaccinating immunocompetent syngeneic mice with dying tumour cells. Compare later challenge with living matched tumour cells in vaccinated and unvaccinated hosts, and test specificity with unrelated compatible tumour cells. Incidence and growth are functional readouts. Immune-competent versus deficient comparisons alone cannot isolate immunogenic death from other immunostimulation. Assays consume tumour-cell aliquots, supernatant or host-model material and report separate dead-cell fractions, signal concentrations or surface staining and challenge incidence or growth. Residual inducer, contamination, incompatible antigens and poor death confirmation can invalidate attribution. No universal DAMP cutoff establishes immunogenicity.

Surface calreticulin, released ATP and HMGB1 have distinct mechanistic roles in defined experiments. Calreticulin supported dying-cell uptake, ATP signalled through dendritic-cell P2X7/inflammasome pathways, and HMGB1/TLR4 supported processing and presentation. These are examples rather than a universal sufficient three-marker checklist. A DAMP is not automatically a tumour-specific antigen.

Death plus extracellular ATP does not establish a cancer vaccine. Danger signals, cross-priming, functional protection, distant control and patient benefit are separate claims. Even a positive mouse vaccination assay remains model-bound and does not select a clinical treatment.

Necrotic appearance can follow overwhelming injury or regulated death mechanisms. A late membrane-integrity measurement cannot reconstruct the preceding death sequence. Histology describes the sampled region; necrosis there does not establish the absence of viable tumour elsewhere, treatment success or a particular molecular pathway. Distinguish tissue appearance from a mechanism established by controlled perturbation and complementary readouts. Inflammation and antigen-specific adaptive immune protection are separate outcomes.

Necrosis describes loss of membrane integrity and tissue breakdown, rather than one molecular route. Overwhelming injury, regulated mechanisms and late secondary necrosis after apoptosis with inadequate clearance can converge on membrane loss. Necrosis is broader than necroptosis.

RIPK3-dependent MLKL activation is an example regulated necrotic mechanism. Sun and colleagues used biochemical and cellular perturbations to establish MLKL downstream of RIP3; a necrotic region or membrane-impermeant dye alone cannot establish that pathway.

HMGB1-deficient necrotic cells produced less inflammation in defined experiments. That result concerns danger signalling, rather than automatic adaptive immune memory. Dye entry after an intervention cannot establish necroptosis, vaccine activity or clinical benefit without the separate causal and host tests.

Histology describes the sampled region; viable tumour may remain elsewhere. A membrane-compromised fraction, qualitative tissue necrosis and method-defined necrotic area answer different questions. Handling, delayed fixation and late sampling affect interpretation, and no universal necrosis percentage identifies a death mechanism or proves treatment success. Preparing and staining a section consumes tissue, while live-cell dye assays use tested aliquots and report a defined membrane-compromised fraction. Clinical morphology and experimental pathway perturbation have different validation contexts.

Senescent cells remain alive and metabolically active while division is durably arrested. Damage, oncogenic signals and treatment stresses can induce the state. It is distinct from death, reversible quiescence, the broader concept of dormancy and immune exhaustion, and is not a synonym for a person's age.

The senescence-associated secretory phenotype varies with cell, stimulus, timing and environment. In Coppé and colleagues' culture experiments, selected secretions promoted epithelial invasiveness; in Demaria and colleagues' mouse skin wounds, senescent cells and PDGF-AA supported repair. Neither experiment establishes a universal harmful mixture or a clinical instruction to remove senescent cells.

Low proliferation and increased p21 one day after stress do not establish durable senescence or a harmful secretory programme. Combine cell identity, longitudinal arrest or regrowth assessment and complementary features such as p16, p21, damage markers and senescence-associated beta-galactosidase. Fixed tissue cannot test later recovery, and no universal marker or arrest-duration cutoff works across contexts. Research outputs include method-defined cell fractions, marker intensities and longitudinal proliferation or regrowth. Stained sections and tested cells consume material. Secretions and their functional effects require their own readouts rather than inference from an arrest marker.

Genetically switchable blood-cancer models showed enhanced clonogenic growth after release from senescence. This supports possible escape in those systems, not inevitable restart, relapse prediction or a preferred senolytic treatment. Arrest, secretion and effects on neighbouring cells require separate tests.

In a phospholipid bilayer, heads face the watery surroundings on either side and tails face a shared inner core. An open ion channel provides a selective pore through that boundary. Net movement of a permitted ion follows its electrochemical gradient, which combines concentration and electrical effects; a drawing of inward flow does not set the direction for every ion or cell. This example is passive transport, rather than an ATP-driven pump or a route for a large cargo molecule. Uptake into a vesicle and escape across its membrane are separate events.

Ferroptosis involves iron-dependent membrane-lipid peroxidation and death. Cystine uptake through system xc- can support cysteine and glutathione availability; it does not transport glutathione itself. GPX4 uses glutathione to reduce lipid hydroperoxides, while FSP1 provides a parallel coenzyme-Q-associated defence. Dependence on these routes varies with the model and cellular conditions. Establishing the mechanism requires appropriately controlled measurements of death, lipid damage, iron dependence and rescue, with complementary perturbations. Findings in persistent or mesenchymal model cells do not establish a universal vulnerability or a treatment recommendation. Necrotic appearance, danger signals and adaptive antitumour immunity are separate questions.

Ferroptosis involves iron-dependent membrane-lipid peroxidation causing death. Erastin experiments implicated cystine uptake through system xc-, connecting cysteine and glutathione supply to antioxidant defence. Vulnerable polyunsaturated lipid chains, iron availability and cellular conditions matter; general reactive-oxygen fluorescence does not establish this mechanism.

GPX4 uses glutathione to reduce lipid hydroperoxides to lipid alcohols. FSP1 provides a parallel coenzyme-Q radical-trapping defence; it does not replace every GPX4 function or describe the whole protection network. Protein abundance alone does not measure protective activity or predict compound sensitivity.

Assigning ferroptosis needs convergent measurements of death, lipid damage preceding death, iron dependence and appropriately controlled rescue. Independent genetic and chemical perturbations strengthen attribution; rescue alone is not complete proof. Probe chemistry, concentration, nutrients, cell density and observation time can alter results. A lipid-probe ratio and death fraction are different outputs, with no universal diagnostic staining threshold. Live death and rescue tests consume viable model material. Specify lipid-probe oxidation ratios and independently measured death percentages over a stated interval; a marker snapshot does not reconstruct the full causal sequence.

A culture with abundant GPX4, a general oxidation signal and no death has not demonstrated ferroptosis. Cell-line and xenograft vulnerabilities do not establish tolerable exposure, selective cancer killing or benefit in patients. Alternative defences can confer resistance, so a strong antioxidant programme is not automatically a treatment vulnerability.

A fictional GPX4 experiment combines lipid oxidation before death, rescue by an iron chelator and a lipid-radical trap, and a corresponding phenotype after an independent genetic perturbation. These observations converge on an iron-dependent lipid-damage explanation; none alone proves it. Include vehicle, rescue-only and an unrelated death condition because rescue compounds can affect other processes. Survival of an otherwise matched FSP1-high comparison is compatible with a parallel defence; directly testing that defence is needed before assigning compensation to it. Energy production, a general oxidation dye and an antioxidant transcript are different measurements and cannot substitute for this causal sequence.

More lipidated LC3-II can reflect greater formation or slower removal. A controlled short lysosomal block and complementary tandem fluorescent LC3 reporter can help examine turnover and delivery to acidic compartments. Equal starting amounts can have different later fates. Little additional accumulation can reflect a late block, low formation or an unsuitable window; it does not establish dependence.

Klionsky's 2021 assay guidelines distinguish LC3 carrier flux from actual cargo or substrate flux. LC3-II is the lipid-attached form of microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3; accumulation can reflect formation or slower removal. Compare treatment alone, a verified lysosomal block such as bafilomycin A1 alone, both together and the relevant baseline, with suitable time and dose windows. An additional LC3-II increase can support turnover under those conditions, but partial inhibition, saturation, low formation or cell death can complicate the comparison. Little change is not a unique diagnosis of an existing late block. A tandem two-colour reporter adds information about acidic delivery, not proof that every cargo completed degradation. Pair markers with an appropriate cargo measurement. Sequestosome 1, SQSTM1/p62, is an adaptor whose abundance also depends on expression and other processes, so one p62 snapshot cannot establish blockage.

Macroautophagy encloses cargo in a double-membrane autophagosome, delivers it through lysosomal fusion and degrades it for reuse. Formation, delivery and breakdown are separate steps; not all lysosomal processes use autophagosomes. Active recycling often supports stress adaptation, whereas autophagy-dependent death requires causal evidence implicating the machinery.

A completed macroautophagosome has separate inner and outer membranes, with space between them. When it fuses with a lysosome, the outer membrane joins the lysosomal boundary, while the inner membrane is degraded before enzymes gain access to the enclosed cargo. Itakura and colleagues located syntaxin 17 on completed autophagosomes, and Tsuboyama and colleagues found that loss of ATG conjugation systems markedly delayed inner-membrane degradation even when fusion occurred. A direct-fusion sketch omits intermediate endosomal interactions described in multicellular organisms; it is not the complete route taken by every compartment.

Product return has evidence in defined systems. In leucine-starved cultured human HEK-293T cells, Wyant and colleagues found that SLC38A9 was needed for leucine made by lysosomal protein breakdown to reach the cytosol; the response also depended on the autophagy protein ATG7. Abu-Remaileh and colleagues measured regulated lysosomal amino-acid exchange in mammalian cells. Yeast experiments identified Atg22, Avt3 and Avt4 as partially redundant vacuolar amino-acid exporters. These results support amino-acid recycling in those systems, without establishing transport of every breakdown product, secretion from the cell or guaranteed growth.

Flux, selected-cargo clearance and survival dependence are different claims. NBR1 experiments identify selective ubiquitinated-cargo handling, not a universal LC3 cargo census. Use time courses, viable-cell normalisation, verified lysosomal inhibition and independent perturbations; autophagy proteins can have other functions. Lower mTOR signalling can change initiation without guaranteeing completed degradation. Typical research outputs include normalised LC3-II band intensity, reporter compartments per cell and selected-cargo disappearance over time. Tested cultures are consumed or perturbed, and prolonged lysosomal inhibition can itself disturb the system. No universal LC3 or flux cutoff selects treatment.

A fictional one-hour recycling-station comparison starts with 20 waiting bags in each station. A receives 30 and processes 30, leaving 20; B receives five and processes none, leaving 25. Equal initial piles, including a six-bag schematic snapshot, cannot identify the rate or the later outcome. Bags are not LC3 molecules or assay thresholds: real markers are produced and removed, cargos differ, and a perturbation can affect several steps. Measure completion over time with appropriate controls. Even verified flow does not establish survival dependence; after a specific perturbation, more death can support a protective role, less drug-induced death can support a contribution to that death response, and changed flow with similar survival leaves timing or compensation as possible limits.

A DNA lesion is a physical or chemical problem; a mutation is a lasting sequence change. Repair can remove damage before a mutation is fixed. Recognition and checkpoint signaling are responses to the problem, whereas successful repair, tolerated damage, arrest and death are separate outcomes. The lesson map therefore ends by measuring the outcome instead of assuming that the alarm completed the repair.

Selected repair jobs address different problems: base excision begins by removing a damaged base, nucleotide excision removes a lesion-containing stretch, and mismatch repair corrects copying mismatches. Lindahl purified an E. coli enzyme that released uracil without cutting the DNA backbone, a specific early base-excision step rather than proof of all human repair routes. Double-strand breaks can use matching-template homologous repair or end joining. These are selected jobs, not exclusive assignments of every lesion to one pathway.

Gamma-H2AX is histone H2AX phosphorylated at serine 139. Rogakou 1998 observed a rapid response after experimentally induced double-strand breaks in mammalian systems. A microscopy focus is a response around damage, not direct sequencing of a break or a universal repair-failure test. In a fictional culture with a bulky lesion and increased gamma-H2AX, measure lesion removal over time with suitable controls before claiming nucleotide-excision failure, homologous repair deficiency or drug sensitivity.

Platinum agents can form DNA crosslinks; interstrand links block strand separation and require coordinated repair machinery. The Fanconi pathway links DNA-processing activities, and homologous repair can contribute to resolving replication-associated damage. This does not mean every platinum lesion is an interstrand link or that every HR-deficient tumor responds. A repair mechanism, an observed drug effect and clinical benefit in a defined population need separate evidence.

Removing a lesion starts a repair job; synthesis and sealing complete it. In a selected base-excision route, a damaged base is removed, the backbone is processed and the gap is rebuilt and sealed. Nucleotide-excision repair cuts out a lesion-containing stretch, then fills and seals the patch. Mismatch repair replaces the incorrectly copied strand segment using the other strand as a template. These are different repair jobs; detecting a checkpoint signal does not demonstrate that any was completed.

Genomic scars are historical patterns in sampled tumor DNA. They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

A repair-gene finding suggests a possible cause, a genomic scar records accumulated consequences, and a functional assay tests present behavior. A variant is not automatically damaging, loss of one copy is not automatically loss of both, and repair can recover while historical scars persist. None of these observations alone is the probability of clinical benefit.

Homologous recombination uses sufficiently matching DNA, often the sister chromatid after copying, to repair certain breaks. BRCA1 helps coordinate repair; BRCA2 helps RAD51 assemble on prepared single-stranded DNA to search and pair with a template. Template availability and cell-cycle state matter. In a fictional model with both functional BRCA2 copies lost, template-guided repair is impaired and alternative joining can leave deletions and rearrangements, but the sequence of a scar does not uniquely identify the cause or every protein that acted.

A low RAD51-focus count is interpretable only with adequate tumor cells, an appropriate cycling population and evidence that the cells experienced damage. Cruz 2018 assessed RAD51 with geminin as an S/G2 marker and gamma-H2AX as a damage marker in patient-derived models and retrospective tumor specimens. Fixed tissue can support this functional-surrogate approach; functional does not always mean live drug culture. An inadequate sample is uninformative, and a research assay needs analytical and clinical validation for its intended use.

Telli tested scar-score associations with response to platinum-containing chemotherapy before surgery in triple-negative breast cancer; that result does not establish a universal PARP-inhibitor cutoff. Farmer demonstrated sensitivity to PARP inhibition in BRCA-deficient cell models, a separate evidence setting. The U.S. olaparib early-breast-cancer label specifies deleterious or suspected deleterious germline BRCA findings, HER2-negative high-risk disease, prior neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and companion-diagnostic selection. A tumor-only result or high scar score does not replace those criteria.

Double-strand breaks can be repaired through matching-template homologous recombination or several end-joining routes. Homologous repair often uses the sister chromatid after DNA copying. The substrate, available template and cell-cycle state affect which route can operate.

Preparing a double-strand break for homologous repair includes DNA end resection in the 5′ to 3′ direction, leaving protruding 3′ single-stranded ends. RAD51 helps a prepared strand find and pair with a complementary strand in matching duplex DNA, displacing the other template strand into a D-loop. DNA synthesis can then extend the invading end using the template. Synthesis-dependent strand annealing can finish as a noncrossover repair: the extended strand leaves the template and pairs with the other broken end. Other homologous-repair routes can have crossover outcomes, so using an intact template does not mean every repair leaves donor and recipient arrangements unchanged. Purified bacterial RecA structures reveal strand-pairing intermediates; they are not direct measurements of human RAD51 repair in a tumour.

Classical nonhomologous end joining reconnects ends without requiring a long matching template and can preserve compatible ends. Microhomology-associated joining uses short matching sequences after end processing. Theta-mediated end joining names a POLQ-mediated mechanism; finding short matches alone does not identify that enzyme. These routes overlap in outcomes without becoming interchangeable definitions.

Ku binds broken ends, and ligase IV with supporting factors can help align and seal them; difficult ends can require processing. Resection exposes single-stranded regions for alternative joining, where short matches can align and intervening sequence can be lost. Purified-factor experiments, defined chromosome-break reporters and controlled cellular studies test particular substrates and factor dependencies, not a universal menu for every break.

A fictional top-strand sequence CA-GAC-TT|AA-GAC-GT has 14 base pairs before joining. A selected short-match product CA-GAC-GT retains seven, losing the four-base TTAA interval and one three-base GAC repeat. For a selected alignment of GAC with its complementary CTG sequence, trimming the unmatched TT flaps leaves seven paired positions and two backbone nicks to seal, without a gap to fill. Other substrates can require synthesis; this arithmetic and schematic geometry are not measured repair frequencies.

Sequence a repaired junction and measure a defined repair reporter, then perturb the proposed factor with specificity controls and, where feasible, rescue. Repair fraction, junction distribution and cell survival are distinct outputs. A deletion with microhomology is compatible with a joining route, but does not demonstrate POLQ dependence, selective killing or benefit from a POLQ inhibitor in a patient. Viable-cell and purified-component studies have model-specific input and material costs.

BRCA1 and BRCA2 name genes everyone normally carries. Interpret a reported variant by its classification, sample and origin, then assess the remaining allele and repair function. An uncertain BRCA2 variant with no normal sample and no remaining-copy assessment establishes neither inheritance nor biallelic loss nor current repair deficiency. Tumor purity and complex copy-number states can limit allele interpretation.

BRCA1 and BRCA2 have different repair roles. Brca1-deficient mouse embryonic stem cells had impaired homologous repair of defined chromosome breaks in Moynahan 1999. Purified full-length human BRCA2 promoted RAD51 assembly on single-stranded DNA in Jensen 2010. These model-specific results do not determine the effect of every human variant; the matching-template diagram omits many preparation and finishing steps.

In the CIMBA analysis, the invasive-breast-cancer results included 3,797 BRCA1 and 2,392 BRCA2 carriers, with individual marker data available for varying subsets. Among tumors with relevant marker information, 68% in BRCA1 carriers and 16% in BRCA2 carriers were triple-negative. These are pathology proportions among cancers in mutation carriers, not the chance that an individual carrier develops cancer or that a person with triple-negative disease carries a BRCA variant. Age and ascertainment matter.

Repair capacity can change after treatment. In the selected eight-person resistant metastatic breast cancer cohort of Waks 2020, four acquired definite or putative BRCA reversions; other mechanisms could restore repair too. A reversion can restore a disrupted reading frame, while old genomic patterns remain. This selected cohort does not establish a common or most-frequent mechanism across all breast cancers, and a single tissue or blood sample can miss heterogeneous reversions.

A mutational signature is a distribution over mutation categories inferred from a catalog of calls. It does not attach an observed cause to every mutation. Several processes can overlap, some causes remain unknown, and a classifier of BRCA-related repair deficiency is not a model of a patient's probability of drug response. Its endpoint and validation population must be named.

Single-base substitutions change one base, doublet substitutions change adjacent bases, and indels insert or delete sequence. In a fictional four-category exercise, template A has percentages 40, 30, 20, 10 and B has 30, 40, 20, 10. For 100 mutations, a 50/50 mixture gives 35, 35, 20, 10; a 60/40 mixture gives 36, 34, 20, 10. The close reconstructions illustrate ambiguity; these are arithmetic examples, not fitted SBS3 data or observed biological results.

HRDetect combines six weighted features, including microhomology-associated deletions, substitution signatures 3 and 8, rearrangement signatures 3 and 5 and a scar index. It is not simply an SBS3-positive call. In the original study, applying genome-trained weights to exome-like data reduced sensitivity to 46.8%; retraining improved it to 73% while adding calls not made by the genome model. Missing rearrangements and sparse substitutions are consequential, so panel, exome and whole-genome implementations require separate validation, uncertainty and fit checks.

Roberts analyzed 954,247 mutations across 2,680 exomes from 14 cancer types; the APOBEC pattern reached 68% of mutations in some samples, not in every breast cancer. HRDetect reported 98.7% sensitivity and 124 high-scoring tumors among 560 breast cancers, about 22%, under its study definition. That selected cohort estimate is not a population prevalence or a clinical response probability. DNA quality, variant-calling errors, signature competition, catalog and software versions remain part of interpretation.

At a moving replication fork, the unopened parental duplex lies ahead of the junction. New complementary DNA accumulates behind it on the parental templates. One new strand is made continuously toward the advancing fork; the lagging strand is made in short pieces that are later joined. Both are synthesised in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction. A shorter labelled track at the same pulse duration describes less DNA copied along the measured molecule, rather than a shorter labelling interval or proof of chromosome breakage.

In G1, ORC binds origins and with CDC6 and CDT1 loads double MCM2-7 hexamers (licensing). At S-phase entry CDK2 and DDK (CDC7) convert MCM into the active CMG helicase (with CDC45, GINS), recruiting polymerases: Pol α-primase starts, Pol ε (leading) and Pol δ (lagging) extend, with PCNA as clamp, RPA coating single strands, and Okazaki fragments joined by FEN1/LIG1. Re-licensing within one cycle is prevented by CDT1 degradation (CRL4-CDT2), geminin, and CDK activity. Oncogenes (MYC, cyclin E, RAS) shorten G1, fire excess and ectopic origins, and cause origin-fork collisions and dNTP exhaustion, the root of replication stress. Chemotherapy exploits this: antimetabolites deplete dNTPs (5-FU, methotrexate, pemetrexed, hydroxyurea inhibits RNR) or terminate chains (gemcitabine, cytarabine); topoisomerase I poisons (irinotecan, topotecan, ADC payloads SN-38, DXd, exatecan) trap the enzyme ahead of the fork; platinum crosslinks block polymerases. POLQ, POLA1 and CDC7 inhibitors are experimental.

Replication stress concerns difficulty copying DNA, including slow or stalled forks. A stalled fork can be protected and restart; it is not automatically a broken chromosome. Checkpoint activation, recovery, incomplete copying, damage and death are separate stages and measurements. High checkpoint-gene RNA or rapid proliferation alone does not establish fork stress, dependence or drug sensitivity.

RPA coats exposed single-stranded DNA and helps recruit ATR through ATRIP, initiating checkpoint signaling in biochemical and cellular experiments. Activated H-Ras in normal human-cell models produced hyper-replication before damage signaling and senescence. Bester studied HPV E6/E7 or cyclin-E-driven models in which nucleotide limitation disturbed replication and nucleoside supplementation in culture improved dynamics. These experiments do not recommend supplements or predict the behavior of every oncogene-bearing tumor.

In a fictional DNA-combing exercise, live cells receive a 30-minute IdU pulse followed by a 30-minute CldU pulse. At the stated example stretching calibration of 2 kilobases per micrometre, a 7.5-micrometre second track represents 15 kilobases copied in 30 minutes, or 0.5 kilobases per minute; a 15-micrometre track gives 1 kilobase per minute. Bester used those pulse times and calibration, but these example lengths are not that study's results and the calibration is not universal.

DNA-fiber measurements require viable cells that incorporate labels; extraction destroys sampled cells. Ordinary fixed pathology cannot retrospectively supply live-label tracks. Document pulse timing, labeling, stretching, track selection, cell-cycle distribution, model and comparison group. A lower population S-phase fraction is distinct from the speed of one selected molecule. Track length alone establishes neither the cause, breaks, restart nor death; checkpoint dependence needs a targeted perturbation and a separate functional outcome, without a universal patient-positive cutoff.

The unfolded protein response has distinct outputs. IRE1-dependent processing of XBP1 RNA produces a potent transcriptional regulator; total XBP1 message and its spliced fraction are different measurements. PERK phosphorylates eIF2alpha and can reduce translation initiation. ER stress also promotes ATF6 proteolysis, releasing a fragment that acts in the nucleus. These findings come from molecular and cell experiments. Branch activity, adaptation, survival dependence and treatment benefit require separate evidence. Specify branch, timing, total protein or RNA controls and direct growth and death measurements.

ER stress is an imbalance between protein-folding demand and local capacity; the unfolded protein response is an adaptation programme, not the same thing as the stress. IRE1 processes XBP1 RNA, PERK phosphorylates eIF2alpha and ATF6 processing releases a nuclear regulator. Distinct branches can alter folding capacity, incoming translation and disposal.

ATF6 travels from ER to Golgi for processing; the released fragment, rather than the intact membrane-bound precursor, acts in the nucleus. Total XBP1 RNA differs from its splice-form fraction. Other kinases can phosphorylate eIF2alpha, so one phosphosite cannot identify the whole response.

Specify preserved material, RNA quality, isoform-specific methods, total-protein controls, timing and identified cell populations. Splice-form fractions, processed ATF6 and defined phosphoprotein signals are different outputs. Increased XBP1 splicing with stable viable-cell counts supports a branch response, not lethal stress; measure growth and death directly and test causality independently. RNA or protein preparations and compatible tissue stains use material; functional dependence tests require viable cells. Report splice-form fractions, defined phosphosite signals or processed fragments with assay-specific controls, rather than a universal UPR-positive treatment threshold.

A mitochondrion has an outer membrane and a folded inner membrane. The space between them is the intermembrane space; the matrix is enclosed by the inner membrane. Each membrane is a phospholipid bilayer, with two leaflets rather than being a single leaflet of a shared membrane. Electron transfer ends with oxygen reduced to water, while some complexes pump protons across the inner membrane. These distinct processes do not give a universal conversion from oxygen use to ATP production.

In mitochondria, respiratory electron transfer and proton movement are distinct processes. Some respiratory complexes move protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space; return through ATP synthase can support ATP formation, while other return pathways dissipate the gradient without that synthesis step. These directions do not specify a fixed proton-to-ATP ratio. Protons return from the intermembrane space to the matrix through the membrane-embedded Fo part of ATP synthase. The matrix-facing F1 part uses the transferred energy to make ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. Protons provide the driving force; they are not converted into ATP. A parallel proton leak bypasses ATP synthase and dissipates the gradient. In Racker and Stoeckenius' reconstituted vesicles, a light-driven membrane system from Halobacterium supported ATP formation when mitochondrial ATPase was included. Their artificial vesicles pumped in the opposite direction to the intact source cells, so the experiment supports coupling without specifying a universal cellular orientation or ratio.

Respiration and ATP generation are related but different measurements. Mitochondrial and nonmitochondrial oxygen consumption, proton leak and ATP-linked respiration require controlled separation. Respiratory transcripts, normalised oxygen-consumption rates and survival dependence cannot substitute for one another; bulk tissue composition and compensatory fuel use also matter. Oxygen-consumption assays require viable cells or functional preparations rather than routine fixed sections and use or perturb the tested material. Report oxygen per time with justified viable-cell or protein normalisation. Equal baseline respiration and different responses to ATP-synthase inhibition do not by themselves identify which culture will die.

In a fictional paired-well example, culture A uses 180 picomoles of oxygen per minute with 30,000 viable cells and B uses 120 with 20,000. Both equal 60 per minute per 10,000 viable cells. After ATP-synthase blockade their corresponding normalised rates are 30 and 40, giving inhibitor-sensitive differences of 30 and 20 picomoles of oxygen per minute per 10,000 cells. Those are oxygen-rate differences, not ATP-production rates or proof of survival dependence. Cell number, fuel, oxygen, timing and the inhibitor controls matter. A corrected, specified conversion method needs additional assumptions; the 2018 Mookerjee correction changed calculations by up to 17 per cent. General oxidation, compartment-specific reactive chemistry and iron-dependent lipid death remain separate questions.

In the selected SREBP-2 route, the precursor spans a membrane and its gene-regulating end faces the cytosol. SCAP escorts the membrane-bound precursor from endoplasmic reticulum through transport vesicles to Golgi membranes. Cleavage releases the regulatory fragment into cytosol before nuclear entry; it does not carry the whole precursor, SCAP or the vesicle into the nucleus. Local sterol sensing and Insig-associated retention regulate this transport. A schematic of the route supplies neither a universal sterol threshold nor a measured transcription rate.

Lipid metabolism includes synthesis, uptake, storage, membrane remodelling and oxidation. Cholesterol regulation and fatty-acid regulation overlap but are not interchangeable. Identify the SREBP member, cellular compartment and measured output rather than treating a transcript, precursor, nuclear fragment, sterol amount and synthesis rate as the same observation. SCAP-SREBP transport responds to endoplasmic reticulum cholesterol in the cited cell experiments. The mevalonate pathway supplies sterols and nonsterol products, including substrates for protein prenylation. Rescue by mevalonate therefore cannot uniquely identify cholesterol as the limiting product. Transcript abundance, lipid abundance, labelled production and a controlled survival-dependence experiment answer different questions. Results from a particular cell model or mouse experiment do not establish a universal tumour vulnerability or a preferred diet or treatment.

SCAP and local endoplasmic-reticulum sterol conditions regulate transport of membrane-bound SREBP to the Golgi. Processing releases a fragment that enters the nucleus and regulates lipid synthesis and uptake. Sufficient local sterol supply can retain the complex in the ER; total cellular cholesterol and SREBP RNA do not measure this processing.

BRD4 is a chromatin reader that recognizes acetylated histones and helps regulate transcription. Its recognition pockets and other protein interactions can contribute different functions.

Engaging an acetyl-recognition pocket and depleting a whole protein are different interventions. In selected TNBC models with acquired BET-inhibitor resistance, cells remained dependent on BRD4 through bromodomain-independent regulation. Verify pocket engagement and depletion independently before comparing growth outcomes. Neither operation alone establishes clinical benefit or a vulnerability caused by an uncharacterized BET-family variant.

BET proteins read acetylated lysine marks; they do not write the acetyl mark. The family includes BRD2, BRD3, BRD4 and BRDT, with two bromodomains and an extra-terminal interaction region. BRD4 can recruit transcription-elongation machinery, but other bromodomain proteins are not all BET proteins and family members are not functionally interchangeable. A schematic that retains the same histone mark during pocket occupation and protein depletion isolates two different interventions. The fixed mark is a drawing convention rather than a measured unchanged acetylation state; the state of the mark needs its own measurement. A representative pocket also does not make JQ1 specific to BD1.

In a fictional culture, an engaged BET pocket probe leaves growth unchanged while independently controlled BRD4 depletion impairs growth. The findings can coexist if the remaining protein supplies functions the probe does not block, as the resistant-model work illustrates. Binding assays, chromatin occupancy, early RNA changes, later growth and death, general transcription effects and appropriate restoration controls answer different questions. Lower MYC RNA alone does not attribute a later effect to MYC.

French identified a BRD4-NUT fusion in the defined carcinoma; a fusion is a different biological alteration from an ordinary sequence variant. Stathis reported four people with confirmed BRD4-NUT carcinomas treated with OTX015/MK-8628 in compassionate use: two had rapid regression, with no randomized comparison or established survival benefit. The report described thrombocytopenia, including reversible grade 3 events and a grade 4 event in one patient. This small selected series does not establish efficacy across BET-altered tumors.

BET proteins contain two recognition domains, BD1 and BD2, alongside other interaction regions. JQ1 competes with acetylated binding partners at these pockets. It was developed as an experimental chemical probe, with binding measured across bromodomains. The original work found binding to both BRD4 bromodomains and other BET-family members; a drawing of one occupied pocket does not make the compound specific to BD1. Compare the actual protein and domain profile of each compound. A preference for BD2, or for one family member, is not comparative evidence of human safety or anticancer benefit. Pocket occupation also leaves protein regions that a separately verified depletion experiment removes.

A BRD3 sequence variant, BRD4 dependence and sensitivity to a compound acting across BET proteins are three separate propositions. A family name cannot connect them without functional evidence. To explain a BET result, identify the reading interaction being perturbed, show which protein functions account for the measured effect and then state the comparative clinical evidence. Decreased MYC RNA is also different from directly inhibiting MYC protein.

A ligand-bearing sender, receptor amount, received signal and growth dependence are separate observations. Locate malignant, vessel and other neighboring cells before assigning a Notch mechanism. Ligand on a vessel is not evidence that the tumor received the signal, and total receptor is different from a released nuclear intracellular domain.

Common contact-dependent Notch signaling begins when Delta-like or Jagged ligand on one cell engages a receptor on a neighbor. Ligand-regulated extracellular cleavage permits subsequent gamma-secretase-mediated membrane cleavage; the released Notch intracellular domain, NICD, can enter the nucleus and work with transcriptional partners. This route differs from an RTK phosphorylation relay and omits receptor maturation and sender mechanics.

Weng found activating NOTCH1 changes in extracellular heterodimerization or PEST regions in more than half of the studied T-ALLs. Agrawal identified predicted inactivating alterations in head-and-neck squamous tumors, suggesting a tumor-suppressor role there. An uncharacterized allele inherits neither direction from the pathway name; tissue, cell identity and alteration effect matter.

A fictional T-ALL culture with high nuclear NICD without a ligand-bearing neighbor, and lower NICD after gamma-secretase blockade, supports a ligand-independent activation hypothesis. A contact-blocking experiment that lowers NICD without changing growth instead supports reduced received signaling without demonstrating a growth requirement. Control general toxicity, contact conditions, independent pathway perturbations and compensation. Gamma-secretase also processes other proteins; responsive HES/HEY RNA and nuclear staining need validated assays and are not universal eligibility cutoffs.

NFE2L2 encodes NRF2, a transcription factor; KEAP1 is an adaptor linking it to a CUL3-containing ubiquitin-ligase complex. Under suitable unstressed conditions, tagging promotes NRF2 degradation. Reduced turnover can make more NRF2 available for nuclear stress-defense programs. Protein turnover, nuclear output, protection against a stressor and survival dependence require separate measurements.

Zhang's biochemical and cell experiments found stress-associated inhibition of NRF2 ubiquitination without disruption of every KEAP1-NRF2 association. The lesson's paired conditions depict altered turnover, not creation of NRF2 or a mandatory physical latch release. CUL3 is a scaffold used with other adaptors and substrates, so a CUL3 change cannot be assigned an NRF2 effect from its name alone.

In a fictional culture, high NQO1 RNA, nuclear NRF2, several responsive proteins and reduced readouts after controlled KEAP1 restoration support a regulatory consequence. Test survival under a defined stress separately, using a specific NRF2 perturbation, matched controls and appropriate restoration to assess dependence. Stronger defenses may confer resistance; their abundance does not demonstrate ferroptosis sensitivity or benefit from an NRF2-directed therapy.

Singh sequenced 54 non-small-cell lung tumors and found KEAP1 mutations in ten, about 19%, alongside a separate 12-cell-line analysis. This cohort proportion is not a universal lung-cancer prevalence. Vartanian's proteomic study in A549 and other cell experiments found that brusatol broadly inhibited protein synthesis, so lower NRF2 after that compound does not establish selective engagement. Use cell identity, preservation, timing, several outputs and general-translation controls; no universal NRF2-high treatment cutoff follows.

E1 enzymes activate ubiquitin, E2 enzymes carry it and E3 ligases help select substrates and assemble modifications. Chain architecture and cellular context influence the result; ubiquitination is not universally a destruction signal. Deubiquitinases can remove or remodel tags, and proteasomal degradation is a later process that needs its own evidence. A protein can fall because synthesis changes, cells are lost or degradation increases, so abundance alone does not identify the route. In targeted-degradation experiments, target binding, E3 recruitment, protein loss, proteasome dependence and sustained cellular effects are distinct observations. Proteasome inhibitors and recruited-degradation strategies intervene at different steps; mechanistic measurements do not by themselves establish clinical benefit.

Ubiquitin is a small protein attached through enzyme steps: E1 uses ATP for activation, E2 carries activated ubiquitin, and E3 promotes substrate selection and transfer. Reticulocyte experiments separated these functions. E3 families differ in transfer mechanism; no single cartoon specifies all of them.

The full-length androgen receptor is a hormone-binding protein that can regulate transcription. Its interactions with other proteins, receptor form and cellular setting affect its activity.

Receptor amount, location, transcription and growth dependence are different observations. Nuclear AR immunostaining reports protein in sampled cells; a luminal androgen receptor, or LAR, label is a versioned RNA-classifier result. TBCRC 032 correlative analyses found AR protein expression alone insufficient to identify AR-dependent tumors. Neither staining nor classifier membership alone proves patient benefit.

Full-length AR has distinct regions for transcriptional regulation, DNA binding and ligand binding. Androgens can change receptor interactions, nuclear localization and regulatory-DNA binding, with effects determined by partners, accessible DNA and receptor form. Tran's antiandrogen experiments in prostate models tested binding, nuclear movement and transcriptional effects separately. An RNA signal does not characterize a truncated protein or transfer those prostate results to breast-cancer treatment.

A fictional tumor with 20% AR-positive nuclei but a non-LAR RNA classification need not have a mistaken result. The assays measure different layers; compare antibody, scoring, tumor-cell content, preservation, sampling, normalization and classifier version. Twenty percent stained nuclei is not twenty percent of patients expected to respond. Dependence requires a controlled receptor perturbation with downstream and growth or survival measurements.

Lehmann 2016 refined TNBCtype from six classes to four tumor-specific classes after immune and stromal contributions explained the former immunomodulatory and mesenchymal stem-like signals. LAR does not mean estrogen-receptor-positive disease. TBCRC 032 was a defined phase Ib/II metastatic breast-cancer study of enzalutamide with or without taselisib, with phase II focused on AR-positive TNBC; its exploratory correlations do not turn an RNA subtype into a universal treatment rule or import a prostate indication.

Class I PI3K phosphorylates a membrane lipid, producing PIP3; PTEN removes its position-3 phosphate. AKT and mTOR are protein kinases. A PIP3 lipid result and an AKT1 Ser473 phosphosite result are therefore different molecular measurements. Document specimen preservation, cell mixture, protein site, timing, exposure, comparator and total-protein normalization before interpreting a change as activity or dependence.

Membrane recruitment helps organize AKT activation. PDK1 phosphorylates AKT1 Thr308, whereas the rictor-mTOR complex supplies Ser473 phosphorylation in the defined experimental route. AKT can inhibit TSC2, relieving the TSC1/2 brake on RHEB, which promotes mTORC1 signaling. The diagram's indirect AKT-to-mTORC1 connection stands for these regulatory steps; it is not direct phosphorylation of mTORC1 by AKT.

Raptor-containing mTORC1 and rictor-containing mTORC2 are distinct complexes. mTORC1 regulates protein production and autophagy-initiation machinery; releasing initiation restraint is not proof of completed recycling flux. Harrington linked S6K activity to reduced IRS-1 function, and O'Reilly observed increased IRS-1 and AKT signaling after RAD001 in cell models and treated tumors. Feedback release can change an output without proving that a combination improves outcomes in every setting.

In a fictional mTORC1 perturbation, lower production-regulator phosphorylation followed by higher AKT1 Ser473 and unchanged growth supports biochemical changes, not essentiality or failed engagement; timing alone does not prove the feedback connection. Test the proposed wiring and functional outcome independently. The FDA's 2023 capivasertib-with-fulvestrant approval specified adults with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, qualifying PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN alterations on an approved test and specified prior endocrine treatment or early recurrence. It is not a TNBC indication inferred from a pathway label.

In a fictional experiment, repair RNA falls, an mTORC1-associated phosphosite falls, AKT phosphorylation rises and more autophagosomes appear. The RNA concerns messages; confirm the proposed protein and repair consequence. A validated site change concerns that output at that time, while the AKT change may fit feedback without proving every downstream effect. Autophagosome amount does not establish completed flux, and no survival conclusion has yet been supplied. Growth and energy inputs also differ: Gwinn 2008 linked AMPK phosphorylation of raptor to mTORC1 restraint during energy stress. Slower costly building work and better survival can coexist. Named S6, 4E-BP1, AKT and AMPK-target sites need their own controls, total-protein context and timing; bulk RNA is not a kinase-activity meter.

Canonical pathway output, dependence on secreted Wnt, growth dependence and clinical response are separate claims. Nuclear beta-catenin can reflect pathway signaling, whereas total beta-catenin also includes adhesion functions. Lower AXIN2 RNA supports an output effect with suitable controls, not selective killing or patient benefit. Wnt routes that do not use beta-catenin are outside this canonical readout.

Canonical Wnt uses Frizzled with LRP5/6 co-receptor machinery. Without an effective signal, the Axin/APC-organized destruction machinery and sequential kinase steps promote beta-catenin degradation; signaling can change that control and allow nuclear regulation with partners. PORCN supplies a lipid modification required for proper Wnt secretion in the studied systems. Blocking that upstream step need not overcome a downstream escape from destruction control.

Two fictional cultures have nuclear beta-catenin. Secretion blockade reduces the nuclear signal in culture A but not in culture B, where downstream bypass is stipulated. A supports a ligand-dependent hypothesis; B illustrates how an upstream block can leave a downstream output intact. The symbols represent qualitative readouts, not protein counts or a real drug dataset. Neither pattern alone establishes selective killing; measure viability and control intervention specificity.

Assays can measure localization, AXIN2 RNA or a defined transcriptional reporter, before and after a specified perturbation. Preservation, composition, global transcription effects, model validation and tissue consumption matter; there is no universal Wnt-high treatment cutoff. In Rodon's phase 1 WNT974 study of 94 people with advanced solid tumors, AXIN2 fell in many paired biopsies while no RECIST responses were observed. Target-related output and tumor response must therefore be reported separately, alongside safety rather than a claim of demonstrated benefit.

Rodon's phase 1 WNT974 study treated 94 people with advanced solid tumours. AXIN2 RNA decreased in 94 per cent of 52 paired skin-biopsy comparisons and 74 per cent of 35 paired tumour-biopsy comparisons; no RECIST responses were observed. These denominators are paired-sample groups, not response fractions out of all 94 participants. A downstream output change supports a pharmacodynamic effect without directly measuring receptor occupancy, selective growth dependence or tumour shrinkage. Dysgeusia occurred in 50 per cent, illustrating that normal-tissue effects also matter. This trial does not justify transferring a target-output change to benefit or a treatment recommendation.

Angiogenesis creates new vessels from existing vessels through endothelial-cell growth and signalling, including VEGF and its receptors. It also occurs in development and repair. A tumour can obtain blood by other routes: Holash and colleagues observed co-option of existing vessels in their tumour models. Vessel structure, perfusion, permeability, tracer transport and oxygenation are separate measurements. Density counts structures within an area; perfusion concerns blood flow through a region; permeability concerns material crossing vessel walls; a tracer readout follows a particular probe. Oxygen availability also depends on diffusion and cellular consumption.

For a vascular measurement, retain the site, region, date, treatment exposure, measured area and counting or imaging method. Vessels per square millimetre describes density; contrast exchange describes a particular transport measurement; VEGF RNA describes expression. None is a direct substitute for oxygen measurement. A vessel-growth mechanism or VEGF signal alone does not establish dependence, selective tumour starvation, safety or individual treatment benefit.

Fictional equal-area fields contain four versus two vessel structures, while separately measured tracer values are 100 versus 160 arbitrary units. The second field has fewer vessels and a higher tracer readout. This is logically possible without establishing its oxygen level or treatment benefit. Drawn arrows are not measured flow rates. A roads analogy or workflow from vessels to delivery organises the questions; each functional step still needs evidence.

Blocking vascular signalling can change vessel integrity and transport as well as vessel number. Tong studied transport after VEGFR2 blockade; Winkler studied a temporary oxygenation and radiation-response window in mouse brain-tumour models. These are conditional experimental findings. They do not establish a universal dose, treatment schedule or clinical benefit, and excessive loss of useful vessels can limit delivery.

Fibroblasts are cells; stroma is a broader compartment that also includes extracellular matrix, vascular structures and other cells. Fibroblasts can produce and remodel matrix and exchange signals with neighbouring cells. In the solid-tumour settings discussed here, a stromal signal is not automatically a malignant-epithelial signal. Sahai and colleagues describe diverse origins and states, without one marker or one effect shared by every cancer-associated fibroblast.

Fibroblasts can produce and remodel extracellular matrix and exchange signals with nearby cells. Their origins, states and functions vary with tissue and experimental context. Stroma is broader than fibroblasts, and a spatial or molecular association is different from a functional or therapeutic result.

Ohlund and colleagues described alpha-smooth-muscle-actin-high myofibroblastic fibroblasts near pancreatic cancer cells and IL-6-producing inflammatory populations farther away in pancreatic models and samples. This is not an exhaustive classification of breast stroma or a permanent job assignment for each cell. Ozdemir reported that depletion of selected alpha-smooth-muscle-actin-positive myofibroblasts worsened disease and immunosuppression in pancreatic mouse models. Removing all fibroblasts is not a general treatment conclusion. The indexed 2015 correction is linked; its body was unavailable for this review, so no correction-specific figure claim is adopted.

A fibroblast assessment may use fixed sections or appropriately prepared cells; sectioning and dissociation consume finite material. Report the defined marker-positive populations, cells per area or another stated denominator, cell states and positions relative to tumour structures. Retain marker combinations, morphology, cell assignment, specificity and sampled regions. There is no universal CAF-high threshold establishing function or treatment benefit. Bulk RNA can increase because there are more cells or because each cell expresses more; dissociation also loses the spatial map.

In a fictional breast section with many fibroblasts and collagen but no scored immune-cell positions, immune exclusion has not been measured. First map the immune cells against tumour nests, then test candidate causes. A neighbourhood drawing can locate fibroblasts, matrix and vessels and suggest possible signals or remodelling. It does not measure movement or show that every fibroblast promotes cancer.

Hypoxia is reduced local oxygen availability relative to tissue needs. It is different from complete absence of oxygen and from a permanent defect in mitochondria. Delivery, functioning vessels, diffusion distance and oxygen consumption all matter, and conditions change across regions and time. Removing tissue interrupts delivery, so collection and handling can change the state being studied.

HIF-1 contains alpha and beta protein subunits. Under oxygen-replete conditions, oxygen-dependent modification of the alpha subunit enables VHL-associated degradation; limiting that regulation can stabilise it. Jaakkola and the Semenza review describe this mechanism and additional regulation. HIF RNA, alpha-protein stability and the resulting transcriptional response are different quantities. Alternative molecular regulation can alter HIF, so neither protein staining nor an RNA signature is a calibrated oxygen meter.

In a fictional biopsy with a high hypoxia-response score, the score alone gives neither an exact oxygen level nor proof that every region is hypoxic. Cell mixture and alternative regulation remain possible explanations, and individual prognosis requires different evidence. Oxygen symbols in a schematic illustrate supply, distance and consumption without measured concentrations or a universal gradient; supply and demand are separate from the response program.

Extracellular matrix includes fibrous proteins such as collagen and fibronectin and carbohydrate-rich molecules such as proteoglycans. Cells produce it; the matrix is not itself a living-cell population. Basement membrane is a specialised matrix, while connective tissue and stroma include cells as well. Production, enzymatic breakdown and crosslinking can change its amount and organisation over time.

Amount, fibre orientation, pore architecture, density, stiffness and cell behaviour are different features. Stiffness describes resistance to deformation, often expressed as a modulus in pascals; the result depends on the measurement scale, preparation and loading. Collagen-stained area and collagen RNA do not directly measure stiffness. Salmon’s viable human lung-tumour slices linked architecture and T-cell movement under the studied conditions; the result does not establish the mechanism in every breast tumour.

In a fictional pair of equal-area fields with eight equal-size fibres each, equal drawn collagen area can accompany different architecture. Independently stipulated mean T-cell speeds of 4 micrometres per minute do not establish equal directions, entry into tumour nests, contact with cancer cells or stiffness. Cell positions outside nests alone do not show that matrix caused them; other signals may contribute. Separate the structural observation, live movement measurement and causal perturbation, then assess any clinical claim with its own evidence.

The tumour microenvironment includes neighbouring cells, extracellular material, vessels and local physical conditions. A neighbouring cell need not belong to the malignant clone. Cell populations, cytokines and chemokines, matrix, oxygen, nutrients and waste interact in both directions, and their arrangement varies between regions, disease sites and times. A drawing is a map of possible participants, not a measured recipe or a fixed job description.

Keren used multiplexed protein imaging in 41 human triple-negative breast cancers to describe composition and spatial organisation. This is observational evidence. Salmon used viable human lung-tumour slices to investigate matrix and T-cell movement, including a perturbation. The two designs answer different questions, and neither makes stromal removal a universal treatment instruction. Presence or proximity alone does not demonstrate signalling, recognition, killing or suppression.

In a fictional macrophage-rich region with inflammatory RNA, composition and expression are observed. The result does not identify every RNA signal’s cellular source, demonstrate macrophage suppression or select the best treatment. A workflow through cells, locations, vessels, matrix and conditions orders questions; it is not a causal chain from cell counts to immune function.

The hallmarks are a versioned research framework, not a diagnostic checklist, stage, clinical assay standard or a demand that every cell independently perform every capability. The 2000 proposal contained six capabilities. The 2011 account retained six, added two emerging capabilities and described two enabling characteristics. In the 2022 account, the two emerging capabilities joined the eight core capabilities.

Genome instability and mutation, and tumour-promoting inflammation, are enabling characteristics in the stated framework; not every mutation matters and not all inflammation promotes cancer. Hanahan’s 2022 additions remain at different explanatory levels: plasticity as a proposed capability, nonmutational epigenetic reprogramming and microbiomes as possible enablers, and senescent cells as microenvironment participants. They are not four equivalent established core hallmarks.

Capabilities can depend on cooperation with surrounding cells. To measure one, specify the process: division, death, invasion, vascular relations, metabolism or immune function. An RNA program is not a direct measurement of every capability or metabolic flux, and there is no universal hallmark unit or cutoff selecting treatment. In a fictional mutation-rich report, an enabling characteristic alone neither establishes distant disease nor proves those mutations caused the behaviour. A framework diagram organises concepts and provisional additions; it does not measure them in a specimen.

Cancer comprises diseases in which cell populations persist and behave abnormally within their tissue context. Normal renewal also involves division, so speed alone, one broken rule or one molecular result does not define cancer. Benign growths can cause harm through their size or location. Blood cancers such as leukaemia need not form a solid lump and can disrupt normal blood production.

In a fictional pair of gene-X scenes, both populations carry the same alteration, but one retains organised tissue relationships and the other shows local invasion. The shared change does not erase that difference or predict identical treatment sensitivity. An epithelial-boundary cartoon illustrates those relationships; it is not a checklist for diagnosing every cancer type.

Local invasion, in-situ disease and established distant metastasis are distinct findings. An invasive cancer need not have detected distant spread. A breast-cancer metastasis in lung remains breast cancer; primary tissue identity and the location of a deposit are different questions. A tissue-family marker alone does not establish malignancy.

Fictional direct counts change from 900 A and 100 B to 90 A and 90 B. B rises from 10% to 50% of the total while falling from 100 to 90 cells. Relative enrichment is not absolute expansion. Any supplied ancestry is separate evidence; the counts do not establish a resistance mechanism or the cause of change.

Sequencing read fractions and inferred cancer-cell fractions are different quantities, affected by purity, copy number and detection limits. Compare appropriate regional or time samples for shared and differing alterations, or trace labelled descendants experimentally, retaining date, location, resolution and uncertainty. An expression cluster is not automatically a genetic clone. A dominant sampled branch does not count every lesion or establish target coverage in unseen disease.

Clonal evolution concerns inherited lineage features and changing population composition through variation, selection and chance. Drivers can contribute to behaviour while passengers accompany them. A newly detected variant may already have existed below the earlier detection limit. Selection and fitness depend on location, nutrients, immunity and treatment, rather than simply the fastest growth or a universal measure of danger.

Nowell proposed an evolutionary framework; Gerlinger’s multiregion study of four renal cancers supplied evidence for branching in its sampled setting. Neither study is a census of every tumour. Genetic drift is chance-driven change in variant frequency, and bottlenecks can change composition without the same selective explanation. A frequency change alone does not identify drift, selection or resistance. Williams tested a defined neutral-growth model in which newly arising variants have no further fitness differences during the modelled expansion, relating frequencies to mutation timing. Tarabichi showed why a good frequency-model fit is not sufficient proof of neutrality or the absence of historical selection.

Normal proto-oncogenes participate in cell growth and survival. Particular sequence changes, extra copies or rearrangements can increase or redirect their activity. Whether an alteration drives disease, creates a dependency or supplies a useful treatment target depends on its functional and disease context.

In a fictional comparison, an overactive receptor supplies a stronger signalling readout while loss of a repair safeguard has a different functional consequence. Neither observation alone demonstrates survival dependence. Interpretation retains the specimen and exact variant or copy finding, RNA or protein consequences and controlled functional endpoints, including exposure and off-target controls. There is no generic oncogene score that substitutes for disease-specific actionability.

Tumour-suppressor genes contribute to growth restraint, genome maintenance and responses to damage. Some cancers disable both useful copies; in other settings reduced dosage or interference by an altered protein matters. The exact variant, copy state and functional context determine what has been lost.

Tumour suppressors can restrain growth, maintain the genome or help remove damaged cells. Knudson’s retinoblastoma model proposed two events, with an inherited first event or two acquired events. Different changes can disable the useful copies, but two-hit loss is not a universal law for all suppressors. Haploinsufficiency means one useful copy supplies insufficient protective dosage; Fero’s challenged p27-heterozygous mice retained an unmutated, unsilenced remaining copy.

A dominant-negative altered protein interferes with useful protein rather than merely reducing dosage. Boettcher demonstrated this for particular TP53 variants in myeloid and leukaemia models, not every TP53 variant or breast tumour. TCGA reported TP53 mutations in 80% of its basal-like breast cancers. Basal-like is not identical to all TNBC, and a genomic frequency does not establish complete functional loss, drug restoration or a current approval claim.

If two adequately tested regions share A while B is found in only one, A is a candidate shared ancestral feature and B is branch-associated under the tested model. A third unsampled site remains unknown. Retain region, date, specimen, method, resolution and uncertainty across multiregion, single-cell, spatial and modelled-fraction studies. DNA outlines, RNA-state symbols and surface marks in a figure represent different layers; icon counts are not measured fractions or treatment-response estimates.

Heterogeneity includes DNA differences, molecular states and behaviour across regions, lesions and time. Clones and subclones describe ancestry; clonal variants are estimated within a stated analysed cancer-cell population. A sampled ancestral trunk is not proof of presence in unseen lesions. Sequencing-read or molecule variant allele fractions differ from modelled cancer-cell fractions, which depend on purity, copy number, detection limits and ancestry assumptions.

Neftel integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, genetic analysis and experimental lineage tracing in glioblastoma to describe four main states and plasticity between them. This is not a universal state map for all cancers. An RNA cluster is not automatically a genetic clone. A population detected after therapy can reflect previously undetected cells, acquired changes or a changed state; two snapshots may not separate these explanations.

In a fictional specimen with 60 target-positive and 40 target-negative cells, perfect specificity for the target can still leave the negative population. A target-rich local biopsy is not a whole-tumour response probability. Even a shared DNA trunk does not guarantee RNA, surface protein, presented peptide or effective therapeutic coverage in every cell. A selected culture can also overrepresent cells that grow under its conditions.

In a fictional immune-pressure comparison, both arms begin with A/B counts of 80/20. Later, the control has 160/40 and the pressure arm 10/40. B is 20% versus 80% of the later populations, although its later count is 40 in both. Recognition and comparable conditions are separate evidence; a larger share does not mean that pressure created more B cells. This example is distinct from 900/100 becoming 90/90, where B’s share rises while its count falls.

Koebel used immune perturbation in chemical-carcinogenesis mouse models to demonstrate equilibrium; a quiet scan alone is not such an experiment. Matsushita combined sequencing, antigen recognition and immune comparisons in mouse sarcoma to support selection of pre-existing antigen-distinct clones. This is different from T cells creating every mutation that appears later.

An editing claim combines longitudinal populations or antigens, recognition or functional assays and relevant comparisons. Apparent antigen loss can instead reflect sampling, detection limits, expression change or another treatment. Neither sequencing alone nor a killing experiment reconstructs the whole history. One immune-rich sample, negative blood test or model cannot assign an individual postoperative phase, explain every recurrence or forecast personal risk; different lesions can face different pressures.

Immune surveillance concerns immune control of transformed cells. Immunoediting adds that immune pressure can alter which cancer populations persist. Elimination, equilibrium and escape describe processes that can coexist or occur independently, not a mandatory three-stage calendar. Shankaran’s genetically defined mouse experiments support lymphocyte and interferon-gamma contributions to control and selection. They do not measure what fraction of all human cancers immunity prevents.

Local invasion, entry into vessels, transport, exit at another site, survival and sustained outgrowth are different hurdles. Dissemination need not lead to successful distant growth. A circulating tumour cell is found in blood; a disseminated tumour cell has reached tissue away from the primary. Neither observation alone establishes an enlarging distant lesion, and regional lymph-node involvement differs from distant metastasis.

A breast-cancer deposit in lung retains breast primary identity, while a separate lung primary is another possibility requiring tissue and clinical interpretation. Imaging and pathology identify represented sites; research tracking and environmental perturbations address different biological questions. Negative findings retain the sensitivity and sampling limits of the method. Arrival, survival, sustained growth and the mechanism maintaining or ending restraint need separate evidence.

A dissemination schematic can distinguish failure, viable persistence and later outgrowth without forecasting any person’s outcome. Its glyphs are symbolic, not measured cell counts. Evidence for a viable state, a maintenance mechanism and a causal reactivation mechanism should remain separate.

Fictional one-week cultures both end with 100 viable cells. In one, no divisions or losses occur; in the other, 20 gains are balanced by 20 losses. Equal final size does not establish equal cellular state. Distinguishing these cases needs repeated viable counts, division and loss measurements, sample or volume denominators and time. Clinical scans, blood assays and controlled environmental experiments answer different questions; no universal negative threshold diagnoses all dormancy.

Cellular dormancy is viable nondivision; population-level dormancy can instead reflect balanced division and loss or other growth restraint. Restricted vascular support and immune control are possible contributors, not proof that every cell stopped cycling. Dormancy is different from death and from senescence or another arrest; low proliferation alone does not distinguish all these states.

Ghajar studied mouse breast-cancer metastasis and engineered microvascular cultures. Stable endothelial niches supported quiescence, with thrombospondin-1 implicated, while sprouting regions enriched in active TGF-beta1 and periostin supported outgrowth. This is a model-specific mechanism, not a universal human reactivation trigger. A quiet scan can mean no cells, cells below detection or restrained growth. It does not prove dormancy, harmlessness, inevitable recurrence or a universal relapse clock.

Damaged bases (8-oxoguanine, uracil, alkylated bases from temozolomide or endogenous methylation) are removed by glycosylases (OGG1, UNG, MPG), APE1 cuts the backbone, PARP1 binds the single-strand break and PARylates itself and histones to recruit XRCC1, Pol β fills the gap and LIG3 seals it (short-patch) or FEN1/LIG1 (long-patch). PARP inhibitors compete with NAD+ and, crucially, trap PARP1 on DNA (talazoparib >> olaparib > veliparib in trapping potency), so replication forks collide with the complex and collapse into double-strand breaks that only HR can fix, the mechanistic basis of BRCA synthetic lethality; PARP1-selective saruparib spares PARP2 and bone marrow. O6-methylguanine, the lethal TMZ lesion, is reversed directly by MGMT; MGMT promoter methylation predicts TMZ benefit in glioblastoma, and MMR is needed for TMZ toxicity. PARP inhibition also traps PARP at oxidative lesions from radiation and generates cytosolic DNA that fires cGAS-STING.

MutSα (MSH2-MSH6) recognises base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops, MutSβ (MSH2-MSH3) larger loops; MutLα (MLH1-PMS2) is recruited and nicks the new strand, EXO1 excises, Pol δ resynthesises, LIG1 seals. Loss of MLH1 (usually by promoter hypermethylation in sporadic colorectal and endometrial cancer, often with BRAF V600E), MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 (germline in Lynch syndrome, or EPCAM deletion silencing MSH2) produces microsatellite instability (MSI-H), a hypermutator phenotype with 10-100x more mutations, frameshift neoantigens, and the SBS6/15/26 signatures. Clinically MSI-H/dMMR is tumour-agnostic for pembrolizumab and dostarlimab; dMMR rectal cancer can be cured with dostarlimab alone (complete responses in >90% of patients in the MSK study); neoadjuvant nivolumab-ipilimumab gives near-universal pathological responses in dMMR colon cancer. MMR loss also confers tolerance to temozolomide and thiopurines (the lesions are no longer recognised). Synthetic lethality: MSI-H cells depend on the WRN helicase; WRN inhibitors are in trials.
